welcome_lead: Today you'll meet alpha, beta and gamma — the three rays that fly out of unstable nuclei.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics Radioactive Decay walkthrough — alpha, beta, gamma, half-life and background radiation.
final_note: You learned the three radiation types, their penetration and ionising power, and what half-life and background radiation mean.

High-energy EM photon, no charge, no mass

walkthroughs.body_html:
Some nuclei are unstable.

They have too many protons, too many neutrons, or just too much energy. To get more stable, they fire out radiation — this is called radioactive decay.

Decay is random: you can't predict which nucleus goes next, only the average rate.

Alpha (α): a helium nucleus. Heavy and +2 charged. Most ionising, but stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air.

Beta (β): a fast electron from the nucleus, charge −1. Medium ionising, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

Gamma (γ): a high-energy photon. No charge, no mass. Weakly ionising but very penetrating — needs thick lead or concrete.

The half-life is the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After 1 half-life: ½ left. After 2: ¼. After 3: 1/8.

Background radiation is the low-level radiation around us all the time. Sources include radon gas from rocks, cosmic rays, food, and medical scans.

mcqs.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
options: Alpha
Beta
Gamma
X-ray

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a natural source of background radiation?
options: Radon gas from rocks
Cosmic rays from space
Nuclear power station waste
Carbon-14 in food

mcqs.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is most ionising?
options: Beta radiation is most ionising because it consists of fast electrons.
The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
Alpha radiation — large, doubly charged particles cause the most ionisation per unit distance.
Gamma is most ionising because it can travel furthest and pass through almost anything.

mcqs.q: After one half-life, what happens to an individual radioactive nucleus?
options: It has a 50 percent chance of having decayed — radioactive decay is random for any single nucleus.
The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
Every nucleus is guaranteed to have half-decayed after one half-life.

mcqs.q: What absorber is needed to stop beta radiation?
options: Beta radiation is most ionising because it consists of fast electrons.
A few millimetres of aluminium (or similar thin metal sheet).
A sheet of paper — beta is only slightly more penetrating than alpha.
Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
